summary: Sets out the operational requirements for root name servers, including hardware capacity, software versions, network connectivity, and physical environment. It was replaced by RFC 2870.

plainLanguage.summary: Root servers are the top of the internet phone book, so they need to be sturdy. This note lists what it takes to run one safely.

questions: what are the requirements for a dns root server
how to operate a root name server
subtitle: The rules for running a bulletproof DNS root name server.

tldr.problem: Root name servers are critical infrastructure that must remain online and fast so the entire DNS system works. Without clear operational standards, some servers might fail or perform poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies detailed operational requirements for root servers including hardware capacity, software choices, network connectivity, physical security, performance targets, and security practices.
tldr.outcome: These criteria became the standard for operating the authoritative DNS root, ensuring the global DNS system remains reliable and fast. RFC 2870 superseded this with updated requirements.

today: RFC 2010 was superseded by RFC 2870 with updated operational criteria, but the principles it established for root server reliability, performance and security remain fundamental to DNS infrastructure today.

sections.title: What Root Servers Do
sections.content:
Historically, root name servers have been operated by volunteers and coordinated by the NIC (Network Information Center). Root servers handle the root ("." ) zone of the DNS and are responsible for all international top-level domains like COM, EDU, INT and ARPA.

The RFC notes that as new top-level domains (TLDs) are created, the set of servers for the root zone may become separate from TLD servers. However, the operational requirements are similar. The RFC is most strict about root zone servers but notes that many of its requirements could apply to any name server.
sections.plainLanguage: Root servers are the top of the internet's address book. When you type a web address, your computer asks a root server "where should I look for this?" Millions of computers ask root servers questions every second, so they have to be fast and never crash.

sections.title: Operational Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC establishes 14 detailed operational requirements covering software, networking, security and performance. All root zone servers must run the same software package (initially BIND), and software upgrades must be coordinated so all servers update within a 96-hour window. This allows the zone master (IANA) to coordinate software changes with zone data updates.

UDP checksums must always be enabled on packets, even though some vendors disable them for performance. The RFC notes this has caused serious problems in practice. Name servers must be dedicated hosts with only DNS service and administrative access, using encrypted login channels like SSH.
sections.plainLanguage: Root servers must follow strict rules: everyone runs the same software, they update at the same time, checksums are always on to catch errors, and nobody can log in except administrators using secure passwords.

sections.title: Network and Security Configuration
sections.content:
Each server must synchronize its clock using NTP (Network Time Protocol) with authentication, using at least two NTP servers. This helps with troubleshooting and security. Servers must send DNS responses with the same source address and port as the request used, and each server advertises only one primary address in the zone.

The RFC requires redundant physical environment protections: servers must be in locked rooms or data centers with restricted access, redundant power supplies (batteries or generators), and redundant network connections so a single line failure does not isolate the server. System administrators must stay current on security threats, audit logs regularly, and be able to detect breakins.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server needs good timekeeping (using multiple clocks synchronized on the network), lives in a locked room with backup power and backup internet connections, and is watched carefully for any signs of trouble.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.content:
As of the time of writing, root servers must handle 1,200 UDP transactions per second with less than 5 milliseconds average latency. The RFC notes that the ability to grow to 2,000 transactions per second while maintaining 5 millisecond latency is highly desirable, as the network was growing rapidly.

These requirements affect both the host hardware and the network infrastructure to which it attaches. Administrators responsible for servers must respond to trouble reports within 24 hours, handle vacations and illness by delegating responsibilities, and provide escalation contacts with telephone numbers for emergencies.
sections.plainLanguage: A root server must answer 1,200 questions per second, each in less than 5 milliseconds. That is incredibly fast. The person running it must be available 24/7 or have someone covering for them.

sections.title: Zone Transfers and Delegation
sections.content:
Zone transfers (copying the entire zone database to other servers) are restricted to local networks and networks designated by the zone master for debugging. The RFC notes that zone transfers can significantly load a server, especially if multiple transfers start simultaneously.

The RFC requires use of DNS AXFR for zone transfers (not FTP or other protocols), and when available, DNS NOTIFY and IXFR (incremental zone transfer) should be supported and enabled. Recursive queries must be disabled for regular queries because recursion causes cache pollution and drains performance. The only exception is when the server needs to fetch missing glue records needed for delegations.
sections.plainLanguage: Other servers can only copy the zone data from specific trusted computers, not from just anyone. The server answers delegations (telling clients where to look) but does not do web searches on behalf of clients, because that takes too much power.

sections.title: Administration and Monitoring
sections.content:
All outages (scheduled or unscheduled) must be reported to the zone master via email. If an outage is not scheduled in advance or is scheduled less than 24 hours ahead, the zone master must also be notified by telephone. The PTR record (reverse DNS lookup) for each server's primary address is specified by the zone master.

The RFC identifies possible selection criteria for where root servers should be located: servers should have low IP hop count to a large number of end hosts, and the set of servers should be geographically and infrastructurally diverse so that failures affecting one server are unlikely to affect others.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the person in charge must be told right away. Administrators talk to each other about the best places to put servers so that different disasters do not take them all down at once.
